The question of whether dogs understand human language is genuinely contested across research and expert opinion. Several neurological studies support meaningful comprehension: brain scans of 18 dogs showed their brains can "detect speech and distinguish languages without any explicit training" [d2], and Hungarian researchers found dogs process word meaning in the left hemisphere and intonation in the right — just like humans — with reward centers only activating when both praising words and intonation match [d3][d8]. Behavioral studies further show that some dogs, such as Border Collie Chaser, can distinguish the names of over 1,022 objects and even infer the names of new objects [d4][d7]. However, other sources challenge the depth of this understanding: one dog training source argues flatly that "DOGS DON'T SPEAK ENGLISH (or any other human language)" and that dogs are overwhelmed by human speech, responding primarily to body language rather than words [d9]. An Emory University fMRI study adds a complicating finding — dogs' brains showed greater neural activation for novel/gibberish words than for known words, the opposite of the human pattern, suggesting their processing of language differs fundamentally from ours [d5]. A further qualification is offered by one source, which states that while dogs can hold a vocabulary of around 165 words on average, "your dog does not understand any particular human language, it is merely able to remember vocables and attach meaning to them" [d6]. Overall, the evidence suggests dogs have some capacity to process and respond to human words and speech patterns, but the extent and nature of that understanding — and whether it constitutes true language comprehension — remains a matter of conflicting research and opinion [d1][d3][d9].
